lines.text: This file is about twelve times bigger than the memory we'll let our programs use.
lines.caption: This file is about twelve times bigger than the memory we'll let our programs use.

lines.text: Ask a simple Python script to read every line into a list and sort it, and it runs out of memory just reading the file in.
lines.caption: Ask a simple Python script to read every line into a list and sort it, and it runs out of memory just reading the file in.

lines.text: Ask the Unix sort command, with the same memory, and it just finishes.
lines.caption: Ask the Unix sort command, with the same memory, and it just finishes.

lines.text: While it works, twelve files appear in a temporary folder, and then they vanish.
lines.caption: While it works, twelve files appear in a temporary folder, and then they vanish.

lines.text: What are those files, and how does sort get away with it?
lines.caption: What are those files, and how does sort get away with it?

lines.text: The obvious fix is virtual memory: treat the disk as memory, and let the operating system keep the parts it used recently in memory, fetching the rest from disk as needed.
lines.caption: The obvious fix is virtual memory: treat the disk as memory, and let the operating system keep the parts it used recently in memory, fetching the rest from disk as needed.

lines.text: But a disk never fetches one number.
lines.caption: But a disk never fetches one number.

lines.text: It fetches a whole block, thousands of bytes at least, and every fetch takes hundreds to thousands of times longer than reading memory, even on a fast SSD.
lines.caption: It fetches a whole block, thousands of bytes at least, and every fetch takes hundreds to thousands of times longer than reading memory, even on a fast SSD.

lines.text: Moving one block between disk and memory is called an I/O.
lines.caption: Moving one block between disk and memory is called an I/O.

lines.text: Once data doesn't fit in memory, the number of I/Os typically dominates the running time.
lines.caption: Once data doesn't fit in memory, the number of I/Os typically dominates the running time.

lines.text: Heapsort and merge sort are both N log N sorts.
lines.caption: Heapsort and merge sort are both N log N sorts.

lines.text: By comparisons alone, heapsort would be at most about twice as slow.
lines.caption: By comparisons alone, heapsort would be at most about twice as slow.

lines.text: But heapsort compares items that sit far apart in its array.
lines.caption: But heapsort compares items that sit far apart in its array.

lines.text: Under virtual memory that array lives on disk, block by block, so heapsort keeps needing blocks that aren't in memory.
lines.caption: Under virtual memory that array lives on disk, block by block, so heapsort keeps needing blocks that aren't in memory.

lines.text: Merge sort reads its input from front to back, and writes its output from front to back, so every block it fetches gets used completely.
lines.caption: Merge sort reads its input from front to back, and writes its output from front to back, so every block it fetches gets used completely.

lines.text: We simulated both under virtual memory on a quarter of a million items.
lines.caption: We simulated both under virtual memory on a quarter of a million items.

lines.text: Memory held a twelfth of them, roughly the proportions of sort's file.
lines.caption: Memory held a twelfth of them, roughly the proportions of sort's file.

lines.text: Heapsort made about twice as many comparisons as merge sort, but more than twenty times as many I/Os: about three for every item it sorts.
lines.caption: Heapsort made about twice as many comparisons as merge sort, but more than twenty times as many I/Os: about three for every item it sorts.

lines.text: Even if every comparison cost as much as a memory access, heapsort's comparisons would take under a second.
lines.caption: Even if every comparison cost as much as a memory access, heapsort's comparisons would take under a second.

lines.text: Its I/Os take more than a minute.
lines.caption: Its I/Os take more than a minute.

lines.text: The I/Os decide.
lines.caption: The I/Os decide.

lines.text: So merge sort is our starting point.
lines.caption: So merge sort is our starting point.

lines.text: It sweeps through the whole file again and again, so let's measure it in passes, where one pass reads and writes every block of the file once.
lines.caption: It sweeps through the whole file again and again, so let's measure it in passes, where one pass reads and writes every block of the file once.

lines.text: Merge sort merges single items into pairs, then pairs into fours, doubling the pieces every pass.
lines.caption: Merge sort merges single items into pairs, then pairs into fours, doubling the pieces every pass.

lines.text: Eighteen doublings take you from one item to a quarter of a million, so that's eighteen passes.
lines.caption: Eighteen doublings take you from one item to a quarter of a million, so that's eighteen passes.

lines.text: But watch the size of the pieces.
lines.caption: But watch the size of the pieces.

lines.text: For the first fourteen passes, every piece is smaller than memory.
lines.caption: For the first fourteen passes, every piece is smaller than memory.

lines.text: Merging only needs sorted pieces.
lines.caption: Merging only needs sorted pieces.

lines.text: It doesn't matter how they got sorted, so each of those pieces could have been sorted without touching the disk.
lines.caption: It doesn't matter how they got sorted, so each of those pieces could have been sorted without touching the disk.

lines.text: So do exactly that.
lines.caption: So do exactly that.

lines.text: Fill memory with the start of the file, sort it right there, and write it out to disk as one sorted piece, called a run.
lines.caption: Fill memory with the start of the file, sort it right there, and write it out to disk as one sorted piece, called a run.

lines.text: Then do the same with the next part of the file, and the next.
lines.caption: Then do the same with the next part of the file, and the next.

lines.text: Our simulated file is exactly twelve memories long, so this makes twelve runs, in a single pass.
lines.caption: Our simulated file is exactly twelve memories long, so this makes twelve runs, in a single pass.

lines.text: That one pass covers everything the first fourteen did, so only the last four remain.
lines.caption: That one pass covers everything the first fourteen did, so only the last four remain.

lines.text: Eighteen passes become five.
lines.caption: Eighteen passes become five.

lines.text: And that's what sort's twelve files were: one run for each memory-full of its file, the last one only partly full.
lines.caption: And that's what sort's twelve files were: one run for each memory-full of its file, the last one only partly full.

lines.text: Each run is sorted, but not against the others, so the runs still have to be merged.
lines.caption: Each run is sorted, but not against the others, so the runs still have to be merged.

lines.text: Two at a time: twelve runs, then six, three, two, one.
lines.caption: Two at a time: twelve runs, then six, three, two, one.

lines.text: Four passes.
lines.caption: Four passes.

lines.text: Watch memory during a two-way merge.
lines.caption: Watch memory during a two-way merge.

lines.text: It holds the front block of each run, and one block for the output.
lines.caption: It holds the front block of each run, and one block for the output.

lines.text: The rest of memory sits idle.
lines.caption: The rest of memory sits idle.

lines.text: So give every run its own block of memory, and merge them all at once: a multiway merge.
lines.caption: So give every run its own block of memory, and merge them all at once: a multiway merge.

lines.text: With thousands of runs, scanning every front for the smallest item would be slow, so keep a small heap with one entry per run.
lines.caption: With thousands of runs, scanning every front for the smallest item would be slow, so keep a small heap with one entry per run.

lines.text: Unlike heapsort's heap, which was the whole file, this one sits in memory the whole time.
lines.caption: Unlike heapsort's heap, which was the whole file, this one sits in memory the whole time.

lines.text: Say run three has the smallest front item: it moves to the output.
lines.caption: Say run three has the smallest front item: it moves to the output.

lines.text: When the output fills, that block goes to disk.
lines.caption: When the output fills, that block goes to disk.

lines.text: When run three runs dry, its next block comes in from disk.
lines.caption: When run three runs dry, its next block comes in from disk.

lines.text: Every block is still read once and written once.
lines.caption: Every block is still read once and written once.

lines.text: So as long as memory has a block for every run, plus one for the output, the merge happens in a single pass.
lines.caption: So as long as memory has a block for every run, plus one for the output, the merge happens in a single pass.

lines.text: That folds the four merge passes into one.
lines.caption: That folds the four merge passes into one.

lines.text: Add the pass that made the runs, and eighteen passes have become two.
lines.caption: Add the pass that made the runs, and eighteen passes have become two.

lines.text: Sort memory-sized runs, then merge them from disk: that's external merge sort.
lines.caption: Sort memory-sized runs, then merge them from disk: that's external merge sort.

lines.text: Merging as many runs at once as memory allows keeps the passes to a minimum.
lines.caption: Merging as many runs at once as memory allows keeps the passes to a minimum.

lines.text: It's exactly what sort did at the end.
lines.caption: It's exactly what sort did at the end.

lines.text: It read all twelve runs at once while the sorted file grew, and then deleted them.
lines.caption: It read all twelve runs at once while the sorted file grew, and then deleted them.

lines.text: Our file needed only twelve runs, and GNU sort merges up to sixteen at a time by default, a cautious setting that trades some speed for less memory.
lines.caption: Our file needed only twelve runs, and GNU sort merges up to sixteen at a time by default, a cautious setting that trades some speed for less memory.

lines.text: That was plenty for twelve.
lines.caption: That was plenty for twelve.

lines.text: But how many runs could one merge take?
lines.caption: But how many runs could one merge take?

lines.text: One per block of memory, less one for the output.
lines.caption: One per block of memory, less one for the output.

lines.text: Real sorting programs reed much bigger blocks than our simulation did, often a megabyte, to cut down on fetches, and a laptop's memory still holds about sixteen thousand of those.
lines.caption: Real sorting programs read much bigger blocks than our simulation did, often a megabyte, to cut down on fetches, and a laptop's memory still holds about sixteen thousand of those.

lines.text: A big enough file needs even more runs than that, so it takes more than one merge pass.
lines.caption: A big enough file needs even more runs than that, so it takes more than one merge pass.

lines.text: Say a file needed a hundred thousand runs.
lines.caption: Say a file needed a hundred thousand runs.

lines.text: Merging sixteen thousand at a time, one pass cuts them to seven.
lines.caption: Merging sixteen thousand at a time, one pass cuts them to seven.

lines.text: One more pass makes them one file.
lines.caption: One more pass makes them one file.

lines.text: So each extra merge pass lets the file grow by that same factor of sixteen thousand.
lines.caption: So each extra merge pass lets the file grow by that same factor of sixteen thousand.

lines.text: In practice, even enormous files sort in two or three passes.
lines.caption: In practice, even enormous files sort in two or three passes.

lines.text: That's why databases sort this way.
lines.caption: That's why databases sort this way.

lines.text: Ask Post gress Q L how it ran a query that sorts more than fits in its memory, and it reports an external merge: the same runs, then merges.
lines.caption: Ask PostgreSQL how it ran a query that sorts more than fits in its memory, and it reports an external merge: the same runs, then merges.

lines.text: So, when data doesn't fit in memory, count I/Os, not comparisons.
lines.caption: So, when data doesn't fit in memory, count I/Os, not comparisons.

lines.text: Work in passes that reed and write in order, so every block you fetch gets used.
lines.caption: Work in passes that read and write in order, so every block you fetch gets used.

lines.text: And cut the passes: make runs as big as memory, then merge as many runs at once as memory has blocks to spare.
lines.caption: And cut the passes: make runs as big as memory, then merge as many runs at once as memory has blocks to spare.

lines.text: Python tried to hold the whole file in memory at once.
lines.caption: Python tried to hold the whole file in memory at once.

lines.text: Sort never held more than a memory's worth.
lines.caption: Sort never held more than a memory's worth.

lines.text: That's how sort handled a file about twelve times bigger than its memory: twelve runs, one merge, two passes.
lines.caption: That's how sort handled a file about twelve times bigger than its memory: twelve runs, one merge, two passes.
